# Intrinsic-measure extension and sharpness certificates

These certificates do not prove the full positive-volume conjecture. They show that, once that theorem is proved with its exact constant, the intrinsic-measure extension follows without additional assumptions or loss.

## 1. Intrinsic dimension and measure

Write the finitely many nonempty fibers as compact convex sets K_z in R^d. Put r_z = dim aff(K_z). A nonempty compact convex set has Hausdorff dimension equal to its affine dimension, and has positive finite r_z-dimensional Hausdorff measure: inside its affine hull it contains an r_z-simplex and lies in a bounded ball. For r_z = 0 this is the singleton/counting-measure assertion. Thus q = max_z r_z is an integer, and

H_q(S) = sum_{z:r_z=q} H_q(K_z) lies strictly between zero and infinity.

The identity follows from finite additivity of Hausdorff measure on disjoint Borel sets and invariance under the isometric embeddings x -> (z,x). Fibers of smaller affine dimension have zero H_q measure.

## 2. A self-contained tube weak-limit lemma

Let K be a nonempty compact convex subset of R^d with affine dimension r. Let B_d denote the Euclidean unit ball and kappa_j its j-dimensional volume, with kappa_0=1. Then, as epsilon decreases to zero,

epsilon^{-(d-r)} 1_{K+epsilon B_d} dx converges weakly to kappa_{d-r} H_r restricted to K.

Proof. Translate the affine hull of K to V, an r-dimensional linear subspace, and split R^d orthogonally as V plus V-perp. At perpendicular coordinate epsilon s, where s is in B_{d-r}, the V-section of K+epsilon B_d is precisely

K + epsilon sqrt(1-|s|^2) B_r.

Consequently, for every continuous function f on a common compact neighborhood of these tubes,

epsilon^{-(d-r)} integral_{K+epsilon B_d} f(x) dx
= integral_{B_{d-r}} integral_{K+epsilon sqrt(1-|s|^2)B_r} f(v+epsilon s) dH_r(v) ds.

Uniform continuity replaces f(v+epsilon s) by f(v) with an error tending uniformly to zero after integration. Since K is closed, the sets K+epsilon B_r decrease to K, and continuity from above of finite Lebesgue measure implies that the measure of their difference from K tends to zero. Thus the displayed expression tends to kappa_{d-r} integral_K f dH_r. The same formulas hold in zero-dimensional factors with counting measure. This proves the lemma.

## 3. Extension from positive mixed d-volume to intrinsic measure

Fix n,d with d>=1 and let c be any proposed universal depth constant for positive mixed d-volume convex-body intersections with Z^n x R^d. Assume that constant has been proved for every such positive-volume intersection.

For a possibly degenerate nonempty S = C intersect (Z^n x R^d), put

C_epsilon = C + ({0}^n x epsilon B_d),
S_epsilon = C_epsilon intersect (Z^n x R^d).

Each C_epsilon is a convex body. Its z-fiber is exactly K_z+epsilon B_d for z with K_z nonempty, and is empty otherwise. Thus the nonempty integer fibers remain the same finite set. Every one now has positive d-volume.

Let nu_epsilon be the sum of d-dimensional Lebesgue measures on these thickened fibers, and mu_epsilon = nu_epsilon/nu_epsilon(S_epsilon). Applying the tube lemma fiber by fiber gives

epsilon^{-(d-q)} nu_epsilon -> kappa_{d-q} H_q restricted to S

weakly. Indeed, each r_z=q fiber has the asserted limit, while an r_z<q fiber contributes an extra factor epsilon^{q-r_z} and vanishes. The total masses also converge after this scaling, to the positive finite number kappa_{d-q}H_q(S). Therefore

mu_epsilon -> mu = H_q restricted to S / H_q(S)

weakly.

For a sequence epsilon_k decreasing to zero choose y_k in S_{epsilon_k} with depth at least c. The union of these sets is bounded, so a subsequence converges to some y. Moreover every point of S_epsilon has distance at most epsilon from S (using the same fiber), and S is closed. Hence y belongs to S.

Fix any ambient closed halfspace H = {w:a dot w >= b}, a nonzero, that contains y. For every delta>0 the closed halfspace H_delta = {w:a dot w >= b-delta} contains y_k for all sufficiently large k. Hence mu_{epsilon_k}(H_delta)>=c. By the closed-set inequality for weak convergence,

mu(H_delta) >= limsup_k mu_{epsilon_k}(H_delta) >= c.

As delta decreases to zero these closed halfspaces decrease to H. Continuity from above gives mu(H)>=c. This proves the intrinsic extension, even when H carries positive boundary mass. No convergence uniform in H is required, because the one limiting y is selected before an arbitrary H is fixed.

For d=0 there is no extension to perform: all fibers are points, q=0, and the intrinsic measure is counting measure. For n=0, the convex-body hypothesis already implies q=d.

Taking c=2^{-n}(d/(d+1))^d proves that the intrinsic version introduces no new difficulty beyond the full-volume version.

## 3a. Reused closed-halfspace depth attainment

Use accepted fact 978e8555ec5bac42 and its outward-halfspace-relaxation argument. Upper semicontinuity and attainment are existing background, not a new contribution in this submission.

## 4. Sharpness of the stated product

Let d>=1, let K be a d-simplex, and let lambda_0,...,lambda_d be its affine barycentric coordinate functions. Its centroid g has lambda_i(g)=1/(d+1). Put S={0,1}^n x K and m=2^n.

For any fixed vertex v in {0,1}^n, the point (v,g) has depth at least gamma_d/m by ordinary continuous Gruenbaum: for every closed ambient halfspace containing (v,g), its intersection with the v-fiber either is all of K or is a closed halfspace cut containing g; the latter has volume at least gamma_d vol_d(K). Every other fiber adds nonnegative volume.

Conversely, let y=(v,x) be any point of S. Some barycentric coordinate t=lambda_i(x) is at least 1/(d+1). Define

L_v(z)=sum_{j=1}^n (2v_j-1) z_j.

For every other cube vertex z, L_v(v)-L_v(z)>=1. Choose M>1 and consider the closed ambient halfspace

H={ (z,u): lambda_i(u)+M(L_v(z)-L_v(v)) >= t }.

Its normal is nonzero because lambda_i has nonzero linear part. It contains y. On another cube fiber its left side is at most 1-M<0<=t, so that fiber contributes nothing. On the v-fiber it cuts out {u in K:lambda_i(u)>=t}, a homothetic simplex of volume (1-t)^d vol_d(K). (For t=1 it is a vertex and its d-volume is zero.) Therefore

depth_S(y) <= (1-t)^d/m <= (d/(d+1))^d/m.

Combining upper and lower bounds proves exact maximum depth gamma_d/2^n. When n=0 the same construction simply omits L_v and M. When d=0 and n>=1, the measure is counting measure; every halfspace containing a point contains at least that point, and the exposing functional L_v supplies a halfspace containing only v. The exact depth of every cube vertex is 2^{-n}=2^{-n}gamma_0.

# Intrinsic-measure extension and sharpness certificates

**Exact intrinsic limit of vertical Euclidean tubes**

If K is a nonempty compact convex subset of R^d of affine dimension r, then epsilon^(-(d-r)) 1_{K+epsilon B_d} dx converges weakly to kappa_{d-r} H_r restricted to K. The normalization includes r=0 and r=d.

Scope limits: The audit explicitly reviews Section 2 and its use in the intrinsic diagonal; it does not independently certify every unrelated statement in degeneracy-lemmas.md.

**Lossless transfer of full-volume depth bounds to intrinsic measure**

Any universal constant valid for positive mixed d-volume intersections transfers unchanged to normalized H_q on every nonempty intersection. Vertical thickening preserves the finite set of integer bases; top-dimensional fibers survive the common tube normalization; a subsequential center lies in the original S, and outward closed-halfspace relaxation retains boundary mass.

Scope limits: Conditional on the full-volume bound being available. This does not establish the OC constant.
